title: I made a dice roguelike for Android with Claude Code and a few AI agents. Here's how that went
author: ZarkonRichard
selftext:
I'm Richard, a solo dev, and this is Dice Charms: Dice Roguelite. You roll five dice, score Yatzy-style hands and collect charms that bend the rules as you go. Play link: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=co.uk.zarkon.dicecharms](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=co.uk.zarkon.dicecharms)  
  
How AI was used:  
  
\- Code: most of it was written with Claude Code. I'd describe a feature or a rule, it wrote the code, I played it and sent back what felt wrong. The design and the calls on what stays in were mine.  
\- Balance: I had it work out the scoring and target numbers before we touched the game, which saved a lot of guessing.  
\- Testing: a separate AI agent installs each build and checks it actually works before anything goes to Play.  
\- Screenshots: another agent captures the store screenshots from the real release build.  
  
What worked: it's fast at turning a rule idea into something I can play the same day. What didn't: it's happy to call something "balanced" when it plainly isn't, so playing it myself still mattered most.  
  
Grade 1 is free, both the Quick and Full runs. Grades 2 and 3 are a one-time unlock. If anything feels off or unfair, I'd really like to hear it.

comments.author: deeplifeaspirant
comments.body: A few fixed-seed runs with expected scores would give the test agent a useful check on charm combinations. That'd catch scoring changes even when the build still plays fine.

replies.author: ZarkonRichard
replies.body: Good shout, thanks. I've got seeded runs for the quick mode but not expected scores per charm combo. Adding a few known seeds with fixed totals is a nice cheap way to catch scoring drift. Stealing that.
